cells.tense: You are leaning toward the pull that fits where you already chose to walk.
cells.ask: Tell one person the direction you're leaning in, then say what you'd stop doing to keep leaning.
cells.core:
You're leaning toward something, and it lines up with the direction you picked. You can feel which of the pulls is worth walking toward, and you're giving it your weight. The fit is yours; nothing needs confirming from outside. Saying it out loud to someone can hold it steady when the week gets loud.

The pull keeps moving, and it comes back through your own engagement. The leaning itself is what keeps both streams running together. What you feed now is the leaning you'll do tomorrow. Genuine interest is the movement here, so follow it without needing to see where it lands. One direction, held — that's the whole of it.
cells.sheetLine: You're leaning toward what you see, and it lines up.
cells.place: where you find which pull is worth leaning toward

cells.tense: You are bracing for a version of this where the two have already merged right.
cells.ask: Let one thing today stay their direction and not yours.
cells.core:
There's a picture ahead where this has worked out and the shared direction is obvious. From inside that picture you push, check, adjust. Talks become chances to pull the other stream closer, and the pulling keeps you from standing here with them. The push costs you the very thing it wants.

When the connection is moving well, it grows without force — care that doesn't drain, holding space without gripping. Their pull needs room to be real without your hand on it. Notice the moment you reach for the outcome; that's the reaching that burns you. Let one thing today stay theirs. See what the room does when you don't steer it.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering the meeting instead of letting it meet.
cells.place: where you find which pull is worth leaning toward

cells.tense: You stood at a door where a real connection was being offered and stayed still.
cells.ask: Say one thing you notice about where another person is drawn, out loud, to someone.
cells.core:
There's a pull you feel and you're not leaning. A moment came when leaning would have been the plain thing, and you stood at that door without walking through. The pull hasn't gone anywhere; the leaning stopped there. In good shape this notices where someone else is drawn and lets that stand without proof.

What's nearby isn't vision. It's letting what you notice stand on its own. Say out loud, to a person you trust or just to the room, one thing you observe about where someone else is drawn. That small act tells you whether the pull is still yours. Comfort with not being sure comes back once you move.
cells.sheetLine: You feel the pull and you've stopped leaning.

cells.tense: You are already steering which pull you'll lean toward, and calling it the room's.
cells.ask: Name one thing you're drawn to right now, and say it's yours.
cells.core:
You're already picking which pull gets your weight — in how you listen, what you set aside, where your attention goes. But you talk as if the direction came with the room. The steering is running; the owning isn't. In good shape, practice moves without force and solitude connects instead of cutting you off.

What's called for isn't a new vision. It's saying the one you already have. Say one thing you're drawn to, plainly, and call it yours. That hands the direction back to the one already steering it, so it can be tended instead of obeyed. The choice was made before you named it; naming just returns it.
cells.sheetLine: You're already steering. You just haven't claimed the wheel.

attempts.check: Each cell makes two claims the record does not strictly support: that the person is secretly deciding whether to lean into a shared direction, and that there's a room or moment behind a stoppage. I avoid the first. Second, the ask in Too Little names Discernment directly, which is a map word; I rephrase it as plain perception of the other person's own pull so the reader can answer back. Third — the Balanced cell's line 'two things that fit' is a metaphor the person may reject; the ask survives, because leaning toward the truer pull is useful even if the read is wrong.
